newsitem.title: INDIA: Train blasts revive Indian worries over northeast.
newsitem.headline: Train blasts revive Indian worries over northeast.

text.p: Twin bomb blasts that killed dozens of train passengers in the Indian state of Assam have heightened worries about security in the country's troubled northeast, officials said on Tuesday.
"The northeast situation is a cause for serious concern," said a senior government official who asked not to be named.

Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda recently offered talks to end tribal and Maoist unrest in the region, where local politicians often accuse New Delhi's rulers of being indifferent to poverty and corruption.
"There has been no response to the prime minister's offer for unconditional talks," the government spokesman told Reuters.

Monday's twin bomb blasts, believed to be the work of Bodo tribal separatists, capped a series of violent incidents in recent weeks in the hilly, forested terrain whose tribal inhabitants are also upset with illegal immigrants from Bangladesh.

The states of Nagaland, Mizoram and Tripura have been racked by tribal separatist movements, while Manipur and Assam have seen Maoist rebellions which have since been contained. Tribal feuds have added to the tension in the region.
Naga tribal separatists in the state of Nagaland killed three members of a state government minister on Christmas Day.
In other incidents, tribal guerrillas killed 22 Hindu settlers in Tripura and Naga separatists shot dead 30 bus passengers from the rival Kuki tribe.
The government official said increased violence only underlined the importance of improving the administration of the remote region.
"For long it has been buried under the carpet," he said.
But a political analyst said this month's incidents did not necessarily signal an escalation of violence, and probably stemmed from reduced security patrols at the end of the year.

"I think that these are sporadic attacks though they appear to have intensified of late because security forces had thinned down for elections and they have not come back," said B.G. Verghese of the Centre for Policy Research.
"I don't think it means basically there is a deterioration in the situation."

He said Indian troops moved to other parts of the region to help oversee general elections in April and May were not redeployed in full strength. Traditionally security is relaxed every year around Christmas, he said.
"The year-end is a good time to let off a bang," he said.
Verghese said violence could also be linked to a water-sharing agreement India signed with Bangladesh earlier this month.
The accord increased the chances Dhaka would help prevent militants from seeking sanctuary by crossing into Bangladesh, he said.
Bangladesh had become a strategic refuge for insurgents after Indian authorities signed a border agreement with Burma to block militants from crossing their borders, he said.

"Sanctuary transit moved from Burma to Bangladesh," Verghese said. "Now, with the agreement with Bangladesh, there is better understanding. This is going to mean there will not be a free run for insurgents."
Verghese also said the militants' apparent coolness towards New Delhi's peace overtures did not spell doom. "I think private contacts are being made," he said.
